newsitem.title: CANADA: National unity focus of Canada election debates.
newsitem.headline: National unity focus of Canada election debates.

text.p: National unity has become the hottest issue of the campaign for Canada's June 2 election as party leaders prepared on Monday for the first of two televised debates.

Heading into the debates -- scheduled in English on Monday night and in French on Tuesday night -- Liberal Prime Minister Jean Chretien and leaders of the other pro-unity parties accused one another of lacking the ability to defend Canada in the next referendum on Quebec sovereignty.
Meanwhile, the leader of the separatist Bloc Quebecois, Gilles Duceppe, was expected to raise the sovereignty issue in the French-language debate in a bid to bolster his struggling campaign.

"It is win or lose for Gilles Duceppe tomorrow night," said Michel Simard, of the Montreal polling agency Leger & Leger. The Bloc was the official opposition in the last Canadian parliament, after winning 54 of 75 Quebec seats in the 1993 federal election.

Political analysts said Chretien was expected to be attacked for Canada's 9.6 percent unemployment rate, but that his opponents, especially Preston Manning of the right-wing Reform party, would try to exploit the the unity issue.
Chretien has been criticized for underestimating the strength of the separatists during the 1995 Quebec sovereignty referendum, which the pro-unity forces barely won by 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent.

"Preston Manning must at the start talk about the economy, but he has nothing to lose by talking about national unity, blaming the prime minister of having done poorly in that regard," said Gilbert Lavoie, editor-in-chief of Quebec City newspaper Le Soleil.

National unity jumped to the forefront of the campaign last week when Le Soleil published a story saying former Quebec Premier Jacques Parizeau was set to declare unilateral independence for the province within days if the separatists had won the October 1995 referendum.
Parizeau quickly denied the report, which Le Soleil said was drawn from excerpts of his memoirs to be published on Monday.

In an interview with Montreal French-language daily newspaper Le Devoir on Monday, Parizeau said he had been prepared to declare unilateral independence for Quebec if negotiations on a new economic or political partnership with Canada went badly.
The 1995 referendum asked Quebec voters if they were in favor of Quebec sovereignty that would include a new negotiated partnersip with Canada.
Quebec's separatist premier, Lucien Bouchard, has said he plans to hold another referendum on sovereignty after the next provincial election.
Parizeau's book provoked harsh criticism from Chretien, a Quebecker and arch-foe of separatism, who said Quebec separatists had not been honest about their intentions in the referendum campaign.
With polls showing Chretien's Liberals heading for another majority in the House of Commons, the controversy may have hurt the campaign of the separatist Bloc Quebecois, analysts said.
